Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 6.pdf ---
SLCCI (Sea Level Climate Change Initiative)
So here's the deal — this is part of a bigger ESA effort, the Climate Change Initiative,
where they're trying to finally make proper use of thirty-plus years of Earth observation
archives instead of letting all that satellite data just sit there. There are about eleven of
these projects running in parallel, each one looking at a different climate variable, and ours
is the sea level one. Basically the science side has already been doing the heavy lifting —
building the algorithms, validating them, running a kind of prototype production setup —
and now we're at the point where somebody needs to take that prototype and turn it into
something that actually runs operationally, day in day out, and can be handed over to the
people who need the data.
What I picture happening is a system that pulls in altimetry data from a bunch of different
satellite missions, runs it through calibration and validation, cross-calibrates between
missions so everything is consistent, and spits out two kinds of products: one is like a
per-mission track of measurements, and the other is a merged, gridded product that blends
all the missions together into one consistent climate record. On top of that there needs to
be a proper archive, because reprocessing is going to happen again and again as
algorithms improve or new calibration methods come out, so we can't afford to lose the
baseline data or any of the intermediate stuff along the way.
The people using this thing day-to-day are going to be on two very different sides.
Internally you've got the folks who actually run and maintain the production line —
scientists who get pulled in when something needs deeper validation or when a new
product has to be defined, people who just judge and sign off on product quality, people
who handle the catalog and metadata, and then the more operational crowd who monitor
the system, handle incidents, deal with user requests, that sort of thing. Externally, the
audience is really the climate research community — people doing climate modelling work
who just want reliable, well-documented sea level data they can trust and build on. We're
not building this for the general public or commercial customers, it's a fairly specialized
research crowd.
One thing I want to be upfront about: we don't need to worry about near-real-time delivery.
There's a whole separate world of oceanographic services that care about getting data out
within hours for things like operational forecasting, and that's just not us — we're purely
about delayed-time and the long, reprocessed historical series for climate purposes, so
anything geared at that fast-turnaround NRT use case can be dropped from consideration
entirely. Similarly, all that formal IT service management process stuff, incident ticketing
frameworks and so on, isn't something we need to bring in here, it just doesn't fit how this
is going to be run.
Cost is a real concern too, this has to be something that's sustainable to operate long term,
not just a one-off build. And it has to be flexible — new satellite missions are coming online

during the life of the project and the algorithms themselves are going to keep changing as
the science matures, so whatever gets built can't be rigid, it needs to absorb new data
sources and let people swap in improved processing logic without everything falling apart.
There's also a push to not reinvent the wheel — there's existing infrastructure out there
already doing something very similar for ocean data more broadly, and wherever it makes
sense we'd rather lean on what's proven and working than build everything from a blank
page. Quality and traceability of the data matter a lot too, since the whole point is feeding
trustworthy numbers into the international climate change conversation, so whatever
comes out the other end needs solid metadata and documentation attached, not just raw
numbers.

Sistema: SLCCI (Sea Level Climate Change Initiative)

Resumo executivo: SLCCI operationalizes the production of climate-quality sea-level records from multi-mission satellite altimetry archives. It ingests, calibrates, validates, cross-calibrates, archives, documents, and distributes delayed-time products, enabling climate researchers to use traceable and consistently processed sea-level data.

Escopo: The system operationally produces, archives, documents, and distributes delayed-time sea-level climate data products from satellite altimetry missions.
  Em escopo: Ingestion of altimetry data from multiple satellite missions
  Em escopo: Calibration, validation, and cross-calibration of mission data
  Em escopo: Generation of per-mission track products
  Em escopo: Generation of merged gridded multi-mission products
  Em escopo: Archiving of baseline and intermediate processing data
  Em escopo: Metadata cataloguing, quality approval, documentation, and distribution of products
  Em escopo: Reprocessing using updated algorithms or calibration methods
  Em escopo: Operational monitoring of processing executions
  Fora de escopo: Near-real-time delivery for operational ocean forecasting — excluded because SLCCI is limited to delayed-time climate records
  Fora de escopo: Public or commercial customer services — excluded because the target audience is the specialized climate research community
  Fora de escopo: Formal IT service-management and incident-ticketing frameworks — explicitly excluded from the operational model
  Premissa: PA-01: Satellite altimetry mission data are available to SLCCI for ingestion. [INFERIDO]
  Premissa: PA-02: Scientific teams provide validated processing algorithms, calibration methods, and product definitions. [INFERIDO]
  Premissa: PA-03: Existing ocean-data infrastructure can be assessed and reused where technically suitable. [INFERIDO]
  Restrição: REST-01 (Operational scope): Products must be delayed-time and historical reprocessed series; near-real-time delivery is excluded.
  Restrição: REST-02 (Cost): The solution must be sustainable for long-term operation.
  Restrição: REST-03 (Flexibility): The solution must accommodate new satellite missions and updated processing algorithms.
  Restrição: REST-04 (Architecture): Existing proven ocean-data infrastructure must be reused where suitable. [INFERIDO]

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - Production Operator (Usuário primário): Execute, monitor, and recover operational processing workflows.
  STK-02 - Sea-Level Scientist (Usuário primário): Provide scientific validation, define products, and introduce updated algorithms or calibration methods.
  STK-03 - Product Quality Reviewer (Usuário primário): Review processing evidence and approve or reject product quality before release.
  STK-04 - Metadata and Catalogue Manager (Usuário primário): Maintain product metadata, provenance records, and documentation.
  STK-05 - Climate Researcher (Usuário secundário): Find and obtain documented, traceable sea-level products for climate modelling and research.
  STK-06 - ESA Climate Change Initiative (Stakeholder externo): Receive an operational and sustainable sea-level climate data capability.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - Delayed-time climate focus: Sea-level products are intended for delayed-time processing and long historical climate records, not for near-real-time operational forecasting.
  RN-002 - Mandatory product families: The initiative provides both per-mission track products and merged gridded products combining multiple missions into a consistent climate record.
  RN-003 - Preservation for reprocessing: Baseline data and intermediate processing data must be retained because products are reprocessed when algorithms or calibration methods evolve.
  RN-004 - Quality approval before distribution: A product must be quality-approved before being released to the climate research community. [INFERIDO]
  RN-005 - Traceability documentation: Distributed products must include metadata and documentation sufficient to identify their origin and processing lineage.

Requisitos funcionais:

  RF-008 - Intermediate-data archiving: The system must archive intermediate data produced by each processing execution. [Must have]
  RF-009 - Processing-version registration: The system must register the algorithm version and calibration-method version used by each processing execution. [Must have]
  RF-010 - Product quality decision: The system must record a quality approval or rejection decision for each generated product. [Must have]
  RF-011 - Product metadata publication: The system must publish metadata and documentation for each quality-approved product. [Must have]
  RF-012 - Approved-product access: The system must provide climate researchers access to quality-approved products. [Must have]
  RF-013 - Reprocessing execution: The system must execute reprocessing using a selected registered algorithm version. [Must have]

  RNF-001 (Reliability) - The system must verify the integrity of 100% of archived baseline and intermediate data objects using a recorded checksum. [TBD] | Métrica: 100% of sampled archived objects have a checksum that matches the recalculated checksum.
  RNF-002 (Reliability) - The system must achieve monthly operational availability of at least 99.5%, excluding planned maintenance. [TBD] | Métrica: Monthly availability is greater than or equal to 99.5%.
  RNF-003 (Flexibility) - The system must permit configuration of one new satellite mission without modification of production source code. [TBD] | Métrica: A test mission is ingested and processed after configuration changes only.

Casos de uso:
  UC-001 - Execute multi-mission processing | Ator: Production Operator
    1. The Production Operator starts a configured processing execution.
    2. The system ingests data from the configured satellite missions.
    3. The system calibrates and validates the ingested data.
    4. The system cross-calibrates validated data across missions.
    5. The system archives baseline and intermediate data.
    6. The system generates the configured product and records status Completed.
  UC-002 - Approve product quality | Ator: Product Quality Reviewer
    1. The Product Quality Reviewer opens a product awaiting review.
    2. The system displays processing evidence and metadata.
    3. The Product Quality Reviewer records an approval decision.
    4. The system assigns status Quality Approved.
  UC-003 - Access approved product | Ator: Climate Researcher
    1. The Climate Researcher selects a quality-approved product.
    2. The system displays its metadata and documentation.
    3. The Climate Researcher requests access to the product.

  UC-004 - Execute reprocessing | Ator: Sea-Level Scientist
    1. The Sea-Level Scientist selects archived baseline data.
    2. The Sea-Level Scientist selects a registered algorithm version.
    3. The system records the selected version for the new execution.
    4. The system executes reprocessing using the selected version.

    1. The Production Operator opens the processing monitor.
    2. The system lists processing executions.
    3. The system displays the current status for each execution.

Critérios de aceite:
  CA-001 - Dado a satellite mission is configured with available input data, quando a Production Operator starts a processing execution, então the system records one ingestion result for the configured mission with status Completed
  CA-002 - Dado an ingestion result is available and a calibration method is configured, quando the processing execution reaches the calibration step, então the system records the configured calibration-method version in the execution record
  CA-003 - Dado calibrated mission data and validation rules are available, quando the processing execution reaches the validation step, então the system records a validation status of Passed or Failed for the mission data
  CA-004 - Dado validated data from two configured missions are available, quando the processing execution reaches the cross-calibration step, então the system records one cross-calibration result identifying both mission identifiers
  CA-005 - Dado processed data for one mission are available, quando a per-mission track product is generated, então the system creates one product record with product type Per-Mission Track and the mission identifier
  CA-006 - Dado cross-calibrated data from two or more missions are available, quando a merged product is generated, então the system creates one product record with product type Merged Gridded and the included mission identifiers
  CA-007 - Dado a processing execution has ingested baseline input data, quando the archive step completes, então the system stores one baseline-data archive record linked to the processing execution
  CA-008 - Dado a processing execution has produced intermediate data, quando the archive step completes, então the system stores one intermediate-data archive record for each produced intermediate data object
  CA-009 - Dado a registered algorithm version and calibration-method version are selected, quando a processing execution is created, então the execution record contains exactly one selected algorithm version and one selected calibration-method version
  CA-010 - Dado a product has status Pending Quality Review, quando the Product Quality Reviewer records an approval decision, então the system changes the product status to Quality Approved and records the reviewer identifier
  CA-011 - Dado a product has status Quality Approved, quando the Metadata and Catalogue Manager publishes its product record, então the system makes the product metadata and documentation available with the product identifier
  CA-012 - Dado a product is Quality Approved and has published metadata, quando a Climate Researcher requests that product, então the system provides the selected product and its published metadata
  CA-013 - Dado archived baseline data and a registered replacement algorithm version are available, quando the Sea-Level Scientist starts reprocessing with that version, então the system creates a new processing execution whose record identifies the selected replacement algorithm version
  CA-014 - Dado three processing executions have statuses Completed, Failed, and Waiting for Input, quando the Production Operator opens the processing monitor, então the system displays the three execution identifiers with their respective current statuses

Glossário:
  Altimetry data: Satellite-derived measurements used to determine sea-surface height and sea-level variation.
  Calibration: Application of a defined method to adjust mission data for measurement consistency.
  Cross-calibration: Processing that aligns measurements from different satellite missions into a consistent record.
  Per-mission track product: Sea-level measurement product produced for one satellite mission along its measurement tracks.
  Merged gridded product: Sea-level product that combines data from multiple missions on a defined spatial grid.
  Baseline data: Original input data retained as the starting point for processing and future reprocessing.
  Intermediate data: Data generated between processing stages and retained to support traceability and reprocessing.
  Reprocessing: Repeated processing of archived data using updated algorithms or calibration methods.
  Provenance: Recorded lineage identifying a product's source data, processing execution, and processing versions.

Este documento é a base de conhecimento fixa (Vector Store B) do sistema de elicitação de requisitos. Ele ensina ao agente
de IA os padrões de escrita, templates, exemplos e regras de qualidade que devem ser aplicados ao analisar documentos 
de projeto.PARTE 1 — Estrutura do Documento de Especificação de Requisitos (SRS)
Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §9.6 · IEEE 830-1998 §3 · Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.

Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK

The presence of an existing system leads to common challenges that both enhancement and 
replacement projects will face, including the following:
■ The changes made could degrade the performance to which users are accustomed.
■ Little or no requirements documentation might be available for the existing system.
■ Users who are familiar with how the system works today might not like the changes they are 
about to encounter.
■ You might unknowingly break or omit functionality that is vital to some stakeholder group.
■ Stakeholders might take this opportunity to request new functionality that seems like a good 
idea but isn’t really needed to meet the business objectives.
Even if there is existing documentation, it might not prove useful. For enhancement projects, 
the documentation might not be up to date. If the documentation doesn’t match the existing 
application’s reality, it is of limited use. For replacement systems, you also need to be wary of carrying 
forward all of the requirements, because some of the old functionality probably should not be 
migrated.
One of the major issues in replacement projects is validating that the reasons for the replacement 
are sound. There need to be justifiable business objectives for the change. When existing systems 
are being completely replaced, organizational processes might also have to change, which makes it 
harder for people to accept a new system. The change in business processes, change in the software 
system, and learning curve of a new system can disrupt current operations.

When old requirements don’t exist
Most older systems do not have documented—let alone accurate—requirements. In the absence of 
reliable documentation, teams might reverse-engineer an understanding of what the system does 
from the user interfaces, code, and database. We think of this as “software archaeology.” To maximize 
the benefit from reverse engineering, the archaeology expedition should record what it learns in 
the form of requirements and design descriptions. Accumulating accurate information about certain 
portions of the current system positions the team to enhance a system with low risk, to replace a 
system without missing critical functionality, and to perform future enhancements efficiently. It halts 
the knowledge drain, so future maintainers better understand the changes that were just made.
If updating the requirements is overly burdensome, it will fall by the wayside as busy people rush 
on to the next change request. Obsolete requirements aren’t helpful for future enhancements. There’s 
a widespread fear in the software industry that writing documentation will consume too much time; 
the knee-jerk reaction is to neglect all opportunities to update requirements documentation. But 
what’s the cost if you don’t update the requirements and a future maintainer (perhaps you!) has to 
regenerate that information? The answer to this question will let you make a thoughtful business 
decision concerning whether to revise the requirements documentation when you change or 
re-create the software.
When the team performs additional enhancements and maintenance over time, it can extend 
these fractional knowledge representations, steadily improving the system documentation. The 
incremental cost of recording this newly found knowledge is small compared with the cost of 
someone having to rediscover it later on. Implementing enhancements almost always necessitates 
further requirements development, so add those new requirements to an existing requirements 
repository, if there is one. If you’re replacing an old system, you have an opportunity to document 
the requirements for the new one and to keep the requirements up to date with what you learn 
throughout the project. Try to leave the requirements in better shape than you found them.
Which requirements should you specify?
It’s not always worth taking the time to generate a complete set of requirements for an entire 
production system. Many options lie between the two extremes of continuing forever with no 
requirements documentation and reconstructing a perfect requirements set. Knowing why you’d like 
to have written requirements available lets you judge whether the cost of rebuilding all—or even 
part—of the specification is a sound investment.

Level of detail
One of the biggest challenges is determining the appropriate level of detail at which to document 
requirements gleaned from the existing system. For enhancements, defining requirements for the 
new functionality alone might be sufficient. However, you will usually benefit from documenting all of 
the functionality that closely relates to the enhancement, to ensure that the change fits in seamlessly 
(region B in Figure 21-2). You might want to create business processes, user requirements, and/or 
functional requirements for those related areas. For example, let’s say you are adding a discount code 
feature to an existing shopping cart function, but you don’t have any documented requirements for 
the shopping cart. You might be tempted to write just a single user story: “As a customer, I need to be 
able to enter a discount code so I can get the cheapest price for the product.” However, this user story 
alone lacks context, so consider capturing other user stories about shopping cart operations. That 
information could be valuable the next time you need to modify the shopping cart function.

User personas
To help bring your user classes to life, consider creating a persona for each one, a description of a 
representative member of the user class (Cooper 2004; Leffingwell 2011). A persona is a description 
of a hypothetical, generic person who serves as a stand-in for a group of users having similar 
characteristics and needs. You can use personas to help you understand the requirements and to 
design the user experience to best meet the needs of specific user communities.
A persona can serve as a placeholder when the BA doesn’t have an actual user representative 
at hand. Rather than having progress come to a halt, the BA can envision a persona performing 
a particular task or try to assess what the persona’s preferences would be, thereby drafting a 
requirements starting point to be confirmed when an actual user is available. Persona details for a 
commercial customer include social and demographic characteristics and behaviors, preferences, 
annoyances, and similar information. Make sure the personas you create truly are representative of

Fred, 41, has been a chemist at Contoso Pharmaceuticals since he received his Ph.D. 
14 years ago. He doesn’t have much patience with computers. Fred usually works

300 bottles of chemicals and gas cylinders. On an average day, he’ll need four new

one will need to be ordered, and one will come from the supply of proprietary Contoso

special training for safe handling. When he buys a chemical for the first time, Fred

Mind the gap
A gap analysis is a comparison of functionality between an existing system and a desired new system. 
A gap analysis can be expressed in different ways, including use cases, user stories, or features. When 
enhancing an existing system, perform a gap analysis to make sure you understand why it isn’t 
currently meeting your business objectives.

the desired new functionality (see Figure 21-1). Identify user requirements for the existing system that

Maintaining performance levels
Existing systems set user expectations for performance and throughput. Stakeholders almost 
always have key performance indicators (KPIs) for existing processes that they will want to maintain 
in the new system. A key performance indicator model (KPIM) can help you identify and specify 
these metrics for their corresponding business processes (Beatty and Chen 2012). The KPIM helps 
stakeholders see that even if the new system will be different, their business outcomes will be at least 
as good as before.
Unless you explicitly plan to maintain them, performance levels can be compromised as systems 
are enhanced. Stuffing new functionality into an existing system might slow it down. One data 
synchronization tool had a requirement to update a master data set from the day’s transactions. 
It needed to run every 24 hours. In the initial release of the tool, the synchronization started at 
midnight and took about one hour to execute. After some enhancements to include additional 
attributes, merging, and synchronicity checks, the synchronization took 20 hours to execute. This was 
a problem, because users expected to have fully synchronized data from the night before available 
when they started their workday at 8:00 A.M. The maximum time to complete the synchronization 
was never explicitly specified, but the stakeholders assumed it could be done overnight in less than 
eight hours.
For replacement systems, prioritize the KPIs that are most important to maintain. Look for the 
business processes that trace to the most important KPIs and the requirements that enable those 
business processes; these are the requirements to implement first. For instance, if you’re replacing a 
loan application system in which loan processors can enter 10 loans per day, it might be important 
to maintain at least that same throughput in the new system. The functionality that allows loan 
processers to enter loans should be some of the earliest implemented in the new system, so the loan 
processors can maintain their productivity.

Each product champion serves as the primary interface between members of a single user class 
and the project’s business analyst. Ideally, the champions will be actual users, not surrogates such as 
funding sponsors, marketing staff, user managers, or software developers imagining themselves to be 
users. Product champions gather requirements from other members of the user classes they represent 
and reconcile inconsistencies. Requirements development is thus a shared responsibility of the BA and 
selected users, although the BA should actually write the requirements documents. It’s hard enough 
to write good requirements if you do it for a living; it is not realistic to expect users who have never 
written requirements before to do a good job.
The best product champions have a clear vision of the new system. They’re enthusiastic because 
they see how it will benefit them and their peers. Champions should be effective communicators 
who are respected by their colleagues. They need a thorough understanding of the application 
domain and the solution’s operating environment. Great product champions are in demand for other 
assignments, so you’ll have to build a persuasive case for why particular individuals are critical to 
project success. For example, product champions can lead adoption of the application by the user 
community, which might be a success metric that managers will appreciate. We have found that good 
product champions made a huge difference in our projects, so we offer them public reward and 
recognition for their contributions.
Our software development teams enjoyed an additional benefit from the product champion 
approach. On several projects, we had excellent champions who spoke out on our behalf with their 
colleagues when the customers wondered why the software wasn’t done yet. “Don’t worry about it,” 
the champions told their peers and their managers. “I understand and agree with the software team’s 
approach to software engineering. The time we’re spending on requirements will help us get the 
system we really need and will save time in the long run.” Such collaboration helps break down the 
tension that can arise between customers and development teams.
The product champion approach works best if each champion is fully empowered to make binding 
decisions on behalf of the user class he represents. If a champion’s decisions are routinely overruled 
by others, his time and goodwill are being wasted. However, the champions must remember that they 
are not the sole customers. Problems arise when the individual filling this critical liaison role doesn’t 
adequately communicate with his peers and presents only his own wishes and ideas.
External product champions
When developing commercial software, it can be difficult to find product champions from outside 
your company. Companies that develop commercial products sometimes rely on internal subject 
matter experts or outside consultants to serve as surrogates for actual users, who might be unknown 
or difficult to engage. If you have a close working relationship with some major corporate customers, 
they might welcome the opportunity to participate in requirements elicitation. You might give 
external product champions economic incentives for their participation. Consider offering them 
discounts on the product or paying for the time they spend working with you on requirements. You 
still face the challenge of how to avoid hearing only the champions’ requirements and overlooking 
the needs of other stakeholders. If you have a diverse customer base, first identify core requirements 
that are common to all customers. Then define additional requirements that are specific to individual 
corporate customers, market segments, or user classes.

The voiceless user class
A business analyst at Humongous Insurance was delighted that an influential user, Rebecca, 
agreed to serve as product champion for the new claims processing system. Rebecca had many 
ideas about the system features and user interface design. Thrilled to have the guidance of an 
expert, the development team happily complied with her requests. After delivery, though, they 
were shocked to receive many complaints about how hard the system was to use.
Rebecca was a power user. She specified usability requirements that were great for experts, 
but the 90 percent of users who weren’t experts found the system unintuitive and difficult to 
learn. The BA didn’t recognize that the claims processing system had at least two user classes. 
The large group of non–power users was disenfranchised in the requirements and user interface 
design processes. Humongous paid the price in an expensive redesign. The BA should have 
engaged at least one more product champion to represent the large class of nonexpert users.
Selling the product champion idea
Expect to encounter resistance when you propose the idea of having product champions on your 
projects. “The users are too busy.” “Management wants to make the decisions.” “They’ll slow us down.” 
“We can’t afford it.” “They’ll run amok and scope will explode.” “I don’t know what I’m supposed to 
do as a product champion.” Some users won’t want to cooperate on a project that will make them 
change how they work or might even threaten their jobs. Managers are sometimes reluctant to 
delegate authority for requirements to ordinary users.
Separating business requirements from user requirements alleviates some of these discomforts. As 
an actual user, the product champion makes decisions at the user requirements level within the scope 
boundaries imposed by the business requirements. The management sponsor retains the authority 
to make decisions that affect the product vision, project scope, business-related priorities, schedule, 
or budget. Documenting and negotiating each product champion’s role and responsibilities give 
candidate champions a comfort level about what they’re being asked to do. Remind management 
that a product champion is a key contributor who can help the project achieve its business objectives.

If you encounter resistance, point out that insufficient user involvement is a leading cause of 
software project failure. Remind the protesters of problems they’ve experienced on previous projects 
that trace back to inadequate user input. Every organization has horror stories of new systems that 
didn’t satisfy user needs or failed to meet unstated usability or performance expectations. You 
can’t afford to rebuild or discard systems that don’t measure up because no one understood the 
requirements. Product champions provide one way to get that all-important customer input in a 
timely way, not at the end of the project when customers are disappointed and developers are tired.
Product champion traps to avoid
The product champion model has succeeded in many environments. It works only when the product 
champions understand and sign up for their responsibilities, have the authority to make decisions 
at the user requirements level, and have time available to do the job. Watch out for the following 
potential problems:
■ Managers override the decisions that a qualified and duly authorized product champion 
makes. Perhaps a manager has a wild new idea at the last minute, or thinks he knows what the 
users need. This behavior often results in dissatisfied users and frustrated product champions 
who feel that management doesn’t trust them.
■ A product champion who forgets that he is representing other customers and presents only 
his own requirements won’t do a good job. He might be happy with the outcome, but others 
likely won’t be.
■ A product champion who lacks a clear vision of the new system might defer decisions to the 
BA. If all of the BA’s ideas are fine with the champion, the champion isn’t providing much help.
■ A senior user might nominate a less experienced user as champion because she doesn’t have 
time to do the job herself. This can lead to backseat driving from the senior user who still 
wishes to strongly influence the project’s direction.
Beware of users who purport to speak for a user class to which they do not belong. Rarely, an 
individual might actively try to block the BA from working with the ideal contacts for some reason. 
On the Chemical Tracking System, the product champion for the chemical stockroom staff—herself 
a former chemist—initially insisted on providing what she thought were the needs of the chemist 
user class. Unfortunately, her input about current chemist needs wasn’t accurate. It was difficult to 
convince her that this wasn’t her job, but the BA didn’t let her intimidate him. The project manager 
lined up a separate product champion for the chemists, who did a great job of collecting, evaluating, 
and relaying that community’s requirements.

Solução
Uma forma especı́fica de satisfazer uma ou mais necessidades em um 
contexto.
Uma solução satisfaz uma necessidade por meio da resolução de um 
problema enfrentado pelos stakeholders ou habilitando os stakeholders 
a aproveitar uma oportunidade.
Stakeholder
Um grupo ou indivı́duo com uma relação com a mudança, com a 
necessidade, ou com a solução.
Os stakeholders são frequentemente definidos em termos de interesse, 
impacto e influência sobre a mudança. Os stakeholders são agrupados 
com base em sua relação com as necessidades, mudanças e soluções.
Valor
O quanto algo vale a pena, sua importância ou utilidade para um 
stakeholder dentro de um contexto.
Valor pode ser visto como retornos potenciais ou realizados, ganhos e 
melhorias. Também é possıvel haver uma diminuiça ́ ̃o no valor sob a 
forma de perdas, riscos e custos.
Valor pode ser tangıvel ou intangı ́ vel. Valor tangı ́ vel e ́ ́ diretamente 
mensurável. Valor tangıvel muitas vezes t ́ em um componente 
monetário significativo. Valor intangıvel e ́ ́ medido indiretamente. Valor 
intangıvel muitas vezes tem um componente motivacional significativo, ́
como o da reputação de uma companhia ou moral do funcionário.
Em alguns casos, o valor pode ser avaliado em termos absolutos, mas 
em muitos casos é avaliado em termos relativos: uma opção de solução 
é mais valiosa do que outra, na perspectiva de um determinado 
conjunto de stakeholders.
Contexto
As circunstâncias que influenciam, são influenciadas e proporcionam 
compreensão da mudança.
As mudanças ocorrem dentro de um contexto. O contexto é tudo que é
relevante para a mudança que está dentro do ambiente. O contexto pode 
incluir atitudes, comportamentos, crenças, concorrentes, cultura, 
demografia, metas, governos, infraestrutura, idiomas, perdas, 
processos, produtos, projetos, vendas, estações do ano, terminologia, 
tecnologia, clima, e quaisquer outros elementos que atendam à
definição.

GABARITO — Project Scenario 6: SLCCI (Sea Level Climate Change Initiative)
Use: "ground_truth" field for RAGAS (context_precision / context_recall).
Each line is an atomic, checkable claim against the scenario text and the
knowledge base — not a full SRS, just the set of facts a well-grounded SRS
for this scenario should be able to cover.

- The system is part of ESA's Climate Change Initiative (CCI), one of about eleven parallel projects each covering a different climate variable.
- The system must take an existing science prototype/production setup and turn it into an operational, day-to-day system.
- The system ingests altimetry data from multiple satellite missions.
- The system performs calibration, validation, and cross-calibration between missions.
- The system produces two product types: a per-mission along-track product and a merged multi-mission gridded product.
- The system must include an archive to preserve baseline and intermediate data, since reprocessing will happen repeatedly.
- Internal users include scientists (deeper validation/product definition), quality reviewers who sign off on products, catalog/metadata staff, and operational staff (monitoring, incidents, user requests).
- External users are the climate research community, not the general public or commercial customers.
- Near-real-time (NRT) delivery is explicitly out of scope; the system is delayed-time / reprocessed-data only.
- Formal IT service management processes and incident ticketing frameworks (e.g. ITIL-style) are explicitly out of scope.
- The system must be cost-sustainable to operate long-term, not just a one-off build.
- The system must be flexible enough to absorb new satellite missions and updated processing algorithms over time.
- The system should reuse existing proven infrastructure rather than being built entirely from scratch.
- Output data must include solid metadata and documentation to ensure quality and traceability.

stakeholders.descricao: Scientists — brought in for deeper validation or definition of new products.
Quality reviewers — evaluate and sign off on generated products before release.
Catalog/metadata staff — maintain the product catalog and metadata.
Operational staff — monitor the system, handle incidents, and respond to user requests.
Climate research community (external users) — researchers doing climate modelling who need reliable, well-documented sea level data.

regras_de_negocio.descricao: The system is one of about eleven parallel ESA Climate Change Initiative projects, each covering a different climate variable — this project covers sea level.
Products must go through calibration, validation, and cross-calibration between missions before being considered consistent.
Reprocessing happens repeatedly as algorithms and calibration methods evolve, so baseline and intermediate data must never be lost.
The target audience is exclusively the climate research community — not the general public or commercial customers.
Near-real-time (NRT) delivery use cases are explicitly excluded — the system only serves the reprocessed/delayed-time data flow.

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a scientist, I want to perform deeper validation or define new products when needed, so that scientific quality is maintained as the system evolves.
As a quality reviewer, I want to evaluate and approve products, so that only validated data is released.
As a member of the catalog/metadata team, I want to maintain the product catalog and metadata, so that the data stays discoverable and well-documented.
As a member of the operational staff, I want to monitor the system, handle incidents, and respond to user requests, so that day-to-day operations keep running.
As a climate research community member, I want to access reliable, well-documented sea level data, so that I can trust it and build my research on it.

As a system operator, I want to reprocess historical data when algorithms or calibration methods improve, without losing baseline or intermediate data, so that the climate record stays accurate over time.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Process satellite altimetry data — the system ingests data from multiple missions, calibrates and validates it, cross-calibrates between missions, and generates the per-mission and multi-mission gridded products.
Review and release product — a quality reviewer evaluates a newly generated product and approves it for release, or flags it for correction.
Reprocess historical data — an operator triggers reprocessing of archived baseline/intermediate data using an updated algorithm or calibration method, without losing prior data.
Onboard new satellite mission — an operator or scientist configures the system to ingest data from a newly available satellite mission.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given altimetry data from two or more satellite missions, when cross-calibration is performed, then the resulting measurements are consistent across missions.
Given a reprocessing run using an updated algorithm, when processing completes, then the baseline and intermediate data from previous runs remain intact and accessible.
Given a newly generated product, when a quality reviewer evaluates it, then the product is approved for release or flagged for correction.
Given a released dataset, when a climate research community member accesses it, then the dataset includes metadata and documentation sufficient to trace its origin and processing history.
Given a new satellite mission becomes available, when it is onboarded, then that mission's data is processed without requiring a rebuild of the existing processing pipelines.
